goals.title: Interactions at realtime, watched in 3D
goals.objective: Every interaction runs on the real engine within 1.1x its simulated duration through to rest, and every stage is done only when it can be loaded into the playground and watched in 3D. Route: wire the fast implicit lane to the viewer, then move the elastic response to a basis computed once per object, then carry fracture on basis updates.
goals.rule: No job may take more than 1.1x the simulated duration of the whole interaction including settling to rest; the playground refuses anything projected over that before it runs (REALTIME_LIMIT in playground/server.py).

rule_met.scene: clamped 8x8x2 glass tile, 20 mm cells (128 cells), 20 mm iron ball at 16 m/s, through fracture, hand-off to Jolt and settling
rule_met.why_it_passes: a 2 ms fracture window, itself 497x slower than realtime, sits inside 8 s of rigid settling that Jolt computes at 0.01-0.03x

rule_failed.why: the exact rank-one eigenvector update costs O(n k^2) per broken bond (13.8 s of a 15.3 s window); truncating the basis loses the cascade, so there is no cheap escape short of a sub-O(n^2) update

modal_basis.accuracy: first-failure set identical to the implicit reference on every scene tested; at the threshold the outcome converges; above it both lanes shatter with matching counts but different pieces (see checkpoint sections 3.1-3.4)
modal_basis.reference_in_same_job: each job carries the implicit Newton/GMRES reference on the same scene as case 2 (8x8x2: 0.12x; 12x12x2: 0.51x)

rule_failed_at.scene: 40x40x2 glass tile, 90 mm ball from 3 m
rule_failed_at.cost_scaling: about N^2.3: PCG cost grows with bonds, iterations with crater depth under block-Jacobi, solves with events

quasi_static.physics_caveat: the quasi-static answer craters the tile and stops the ball where the dynamic reference shatters it (8x8x2: 156 bonds, 1 piece vs 400-912 bonds, 2-30 pieces; first-failure sets disjoint; only removed energy agrees, within 11-29%). It meets the rule; it does not reproduce the dynamic outcome.

gpu_lattice.commit: 7d07996 (final doc commit pending the last scaling rows)
gpu_lattice.what_it_is: the CPU lane physics (BrittleBondSolver) and the shared BondFailure criterion executed bit for bit on a colour-parallel schedule, with a CUDA backend behind BANJO_BUILD_CUDA (default OFF) and a CPU backend that always builds; equality proven: max |du| = 0 GPU vs CPU through a fracture cascade, max |dx| = 4.0e-11 m vs BrittleBondSolver with identical first-failure set, pieces and energy

rule_met.scene: 192-cell uniform-cube glass tile (0.24 x 0.04 x 0.16 m, 20 mm cells, 1,704 bonds) on two ledges, 4 cm iron ball at 8 m/s, through fracture (7,288 substeps at 1.59 us, the window itself resolved), hand-off and settling

rule_failed.1536_cells_glass: about 7x (the cascade fills the whole 200 ms lattice window at 142-155 us per substep)
rule_failed.oak_iron_1536_cells: pass at 0.76x and 0.59x because their cascades end within 15-21 ms

gpu_lattice.throughput: GPU 55 M bond-updates/s at 192 cells, no faster than this lane single-threaded CPU backend (57-68 M; BrittleBondSolver itself 19-21 M; the network lane 0.85 M); the GPU overtakes one core from 384 cells (1.9x) and reaches 616 M at 173k bonds, five times short of the ~3e9 the brief estimated
gpu_lattice.obstacle: structural: one Gauss-Seidel substep is a chain of 22-32 node-disjoint colour stages, each a barrier, costing 25-35 us on one block regardless of bond count below 20k bonds, while the substep advances 0.3-1.6 us of simulated time
gpu_lattice.significance: this is the only lane where the fracture window itself is computed at its resolved step and the rule still holds; at 192 cells even its CPU backend in double meets the rule (0.41x). physical_response_validated stays false; the outcome is not converged with respect to sweep order, precision or cell size.
